late one night In 1909, while the Estus Warat steamed for Durban, South Africa, a first class passenger named Claude G. Sawyer rose from his birth and walked on deck. The sea churned and the sky burned crimson. Then on the horizon, a hellish figure rose from the sea, swinging a sword with one hand and clutching a blood soaked rag in the other. As the apparition grew near, he called out Warata again and again until Sawyer finally awoke from the nightmare. The next morning, he couldn't shake the sense of dread. And night after night, he had the same terrible dream, the same spectre, crying out the word war over and over. When they arrived in Durban, Sawyer left the ship for good, ending his voyage early. He would continue his trip to Cape Town in another liner. Only a few days later, the S's Warat with 211 souls on board would vanish without a trace. In 1869, William Lond founded the Blue Anchor Line. The company operated a fleet of sailing ships that primarily serviced routes between London, South Africa, and Australia. By 1890, Lond and his sons replaced their fleet of sailing ships with versatile steamers designed to carry both cargo and passengers. The Lion's livery featured a black and white funnel with a distinctive blue anchor design. In 1907, the Lond family commissioned a new cargo and passenger vessel with the shipyard Barklay Curl and Company of Glasgow. The design was modeled after the SSG, a 7,700 ton liner launched in 1904. But this new liner would be nearly 2,000 tons larger, making her the largest and most luxurious ship in the Blue Anchor fleet. Yard number 472 was launched on September 12th, 1908, encryed by Mrs. JW Taverner, wife of the agent general of Victoria and a person whose first name no one seemed to think important enough to write down. The SS Warita came in at 9,339 tons with a length of 465 ft and a beam of just over 59 ft. She was powered by two sets of quadruple expansion steam engines that drove two screw propellers, achieving a speed of 13 1/2 knots. She was equipped with a double bottom and her hole was divided into eight watertight compartments. She featured luxurious accommodations for up to 128 first class passengers with welle equipped staterooms, a saloon, and a music lounge. Her thirdass accommodations could hold up to 300 passengers. In addition to these spaces, the Warata was designed to function as an immigrant ship with cargo holds that could easily be converted into dormitories capable of holding up to 700 steerage passengers on outward voyages. in general cargo on return trips to London. She was operated by a crew of 154. After a successful set of sea trials held on October 23rd, 1908, she was turned over to her new owners and immediately began her short career. She left London on her maiden voyage on November 5th, 1908. commanded by Captain Joshua Edward Ilbury, a veteran of the Blueest Star line with over 30 years of experience. During this first voyage, she suffered an engine room fire that was quickly brought under control and repairs were made in Sydney. She completed the voyage, returning to London on March 7th, 1909. Upon his return, Captain Ilbury was apparently not completely satisfied with the ship and was said to have reported that she suffered stability issues, making it especially difficult to properly load her cargo. In hindsight, it's difficult to know the extent of Captain Il's concerns, which would be scrutinized by the later inquiry and heavily sensationalized by the press. Ilbury was an experienced and wellrespected captain. And despite whatever concerns he might have had, he considered the war safe enough to embark on her second voyage. A voyage that would prove to be her last war is a species of flower native to the southeastern part of Australia and a state emblem of New South Wales. The name Warata comes from the Yora Aboriginal people who inhabited the area that would become Sydney. In 1848, a ship bearing the name Warat was lost in the English Channel. Another was lost on a voyage to Sydney in 1887, and yet another was lost in the Gulf of Carpentaria in 1897. In total, at least four vessels with the unlucky name were lost before the blue anchor lines Warat sailed her final voyage in 1909. This voyage was only the Warahas second, leaving London on April 27th, 1909. The first few legs were uneventful as she made her stops in South Africa, but she faced severe gales as she made her way from Adelaide to Melbourne. She reached Sydney in June without any damage or noteworthy issues. She departed Sydney loaded with 7,800 bars of bullion, wool, frozen meat, dairy, and flour on June 26th and picked up additional cargo and passengers in Adelaide and Melbourne. She left Australia on July 7th with about 100 passengers bound for her stops in South Africa. During this leg of the voyage, first class passenger Claude Gustav Sawyer, a Swissborn engineer living with his family in Sussex, grew concerned about the ship's stability. He claimed that even in calm seas, the ship had a considerable list to starboard and would unexpectedly recover with a sudden jerk so violent that it injured two passengers. Mrs. Cawwood would also disembark in Durban and Mrs. Lasslo, as well as the ship's surgeon, Dr. Howard Fulford. Mr. Sawyer was a well-educated and seasoned traveler. He understood how a properly designed ship should behave in a variety of conditions. He made it widely known to his fellow passengers that he was convinced the Warat was an unhappy ship. But as the liner continued, her everpresent list had eased to only a few degrees. And soon Mr. Sawyer nearly forgot about his concerns altogether. But then three or four days out of Durban, he dreamed of the strange apparition with a sword and a blood soaked rag. He would have the same nightmare each of his remaining nights aboard the ship. Another passenger, Mr. Eworth, when asked about what he made of the vision, said that it was probably a warning. This was enough for Mr. Sawyer, and he decided that he would get off the ship in Durban and finish his journey on another liner. He tried to convince other passengers to do the same, but no one joined him. Claude Sawyer left the ship when she arrived in Durban on the morning of July 25th. The next day, the SS Warita left Durban, bound for Cape Town, South Africa. Mr. Sawyer had one last nightmare a few days later on July 28th. He saw the ship in the distance, fighting through heavy seas when a huge wave swept over her, rolling her onto her starboard side. She soon disappeared beneath the waves. The war was expected to reach Cape Town on the 29th of July. She never reached her destination. Her disappearance launched a considerable search effort, numerous claimed sightings, and wild speculation over what could have happened to the brand new liner in the 211 souls on board. The last confirmed sighting of the SS Warita came from the steamship clan McIntyre at around 4:00 on July 27th. The two vessels communicated by signal lamp as the newer and faster Warat overtook the older steamer near the mouth of the Vashy River and eventually faded into the horizon. At 9:30, the weather in the area deteriorated rapidly and a storm rolled in the next day on July 28th. The captain of the clan McIntyre would later report that it was some of the worst conditions that he had ever experienced in his 13 years at sea. As the war scheduled arrival time came and went, concerns slowly grew. It was not uncommon at the time for a vessel to arrive a day or two behind schedule. While the Warita was a new and modern ship, she was not equipped with a wireless set, leaving her to face emergencies on her own. But as the days turned into weeks, theories and rumors spread like wildfire through the public and the press. The war was considered by some to be unsinkable. This was 3 years before the Titanic disaster would call modern safety features into question. So at this point, confidence in ship design was at an all-time high. And War featured a modern design with watertight compartments and a double bottom. She was also provisioned with enough supplies in her cargo holds to comfortably sustain her passengers and crew for months. So the prevailing theory was that she lost power at some point during her voyage and was now set helplessly a drift. This was bolstered by an incident involving the Essis Wakado in 1899. The vessel broke down off the coast of Cape Town and drifted 2,500 m over the course of 100 days before finally being rescued. The tugboat TE Fuller was the first vessel sent to search for the lost liner on August 1st, but they were soon forced to return due to harsh weather. The search quickly resumed and was joined by the Royal Navy cruisers HMS Pandora, Forte, and Hermes. They concentrated in the area where she was last spotted, but encountered waves so large that HMS Hermes suffered hole damage and had to be placed in dry dock for repairs. On August 10th, a report of a blue anchor line ship slowly making its way for Durban raised hopes, but this proved to be a false report. In September 1909, the Blue Anchor Line chartered the Union Castle cargo ship Sabine to conduct a search that covered 14,000 m, but nothing was found. On December 15th, 1909, over 4 months after the liner vanished, Lloyds of London officially posted the Wars missing. But soon after in 1910, relatives of the Waratas passengers sent another search party in a desperate attempt to find the missing ship. They chartered the Wakefield, which would spend another 4 months searching, covering an additional 15,000 m. But again, despite these exhaustive efforts, no trace of the missing Warat or her passengers was ever found. >> >> In December 1910, the Board of Trade conducted an official inquiry into the disappearance of the Warat. But with a lack of evidence or witness testimony, they struggled to find a definitive explanation for the disaster. In the years that followed, numerous theories have been entertained, but there are two that seem to carry the most weight. The first and most popular is that the ship was topheavy and prone to stability issues that proved catastrophic in the heavy seas no doubt faced after she overtook the clan McIntyre on July 27th. The official inquiry spent much of its time going over the plausibility of this theory. The Warat was based heavily on the design for the Gilong, which by this point had been sailing for years and had proven itself a safe and reliable vessel. Numerous expert witnesses agreed that she was built and designed properly. And she also just passed numerous inspections by her builders, her owners, the board of trade, and two separate inspections from Lloyds of London, which gave her their top rating. Still, rumors of instability persisted from passengers on her maiden voyage and others familiar with the vessel. One former passenger even reported that it was impossible to take bass on the ships at times due to the severe and persistent list. There was also of course the testimony of Mr. Sawyer who was so concerned by these issues that he left the ship. But for all the accounts of stability issues that came out during the inquiry, there were just as many accounts praising the ship and her performance. Agnes Haye, a passenger on the Warat's ill- fated final voyage, was actually also a passenger on her first. She wrote to friends and family telling them how satisfactory she found the ship and complimented the officers and crew. Clearly, she was confident enough in the liner to book passage for a second voyage. If Warah was plagued by such severe stability issues, how did she clear every inspection? Why did passengers, crew, and officers remark on how fine of a ship she was? And why would Captain Ilbury, an experienced and wellrespected captain, deem her safe? At the time, it wasn't all that uncommon for passenger ships to be slightly topheavy. Even major transatlantic liners. The Emperor, for example, built a few years later, was famously unstable, earning the nickname Limper. And even the RMS Queen Mary was famous for rolling in heavy seas. So it's hard to know whether a handful of passengers were reacting in hindsight to perhaps heavy but somewhat normal rolling or if the warat in fact did suffer a significant design flaw that left her vulnerable to capsizing. If she was unstable, it's a terrifying sight to imagine as she would likely have gone over in minutes or even seconds. the people on board would have almost no time at all to comprehend what was happening or attempt an escape. But there's another chilling theory that gets less attention now, though it saw considerable speculation in the press of the time. This was that the war suffered an explosion that caused the liner to sink almost instantly. One disputed eyewitness account gives credence to this theory. At around 7:30 p.m. on July 27th, Captain John Bruce of a ship called the Harlo and other members of his crew saw two mass lights 10 m away from a ship emitting an abnormally large amount of smoke. The Harlo's chief engineer also cited the ship, but he claimed that it was much closer. Soon after, they saw two broad fan tail flashes on the horizon that they thought were likely caused by a bunker or a boiler explosion. The lights and smoke from the nearby ship vanished almost immediately after the blast. The most glaring issue with the Harlo sighting is that its location contradicts the confirmed sighting from the clan McIntyre. Is the McIntyre communicated with the Warat further along in their course to Cape Town hours earlier that same day. The only way the Harlo could have seen the war at the coordinates Captain Bruce provided is if the Warat for some reason turned back to Durban. Captain Bruce and his crew were adamant about what they saw. And the captain even went so far as to suggest they run a wire to search for the wreck 3 to four miles from the mouth of the St. John River where they saw the burning ship explode. A boiler explosion might not be as far-fetched as it sounds, especially considering that the war toss suffered an engine room fire not long before. It's possible that the fire left more damage to one of her boilers than what was detected at the time, leading to an eventual explosion. While nothing was ever officially confirmed, there were some reports of charred wreckage found in the area. Explosions at sea have been known to quickly claim vessels, leaving minimal debris on the surface. But with all of this, it's important to take these accounts with a grain of salt. Many were recollections from months after the events took place. Many were relayed through newspaper accounts looking to report a dramatic story. and many have been distorted by the passage of time. The war disaster proved devastating for the blue anchor line. Their reputation never recovered from the incident and they eventually sold their fleet to PNO. The ultimate fate of the Warat remains unsolved. All that leaves us with only one certainty. We will probably never know what really happened to the 211 souls who vanished with the Warita over a century ago. Numerous efforts to find a wreck over the years so far have proven unsuccessful. And with the vastness of the sea and the passage of time, it's likely that she will never be found. Perhaps it makes no difference to the people who lost their lives, but to us the uncertainty of tragedies like the war, nod our desire to understand the world we live in. If something happens to someone we love, we want to know why. We want a complete story, a satisfying ending. But as our tools to make sense of the world fail, the unknowns pile up. We're left to drift, wondering what will come for us. >> >> Thank you so much for watching. If you enjoyed this one, help out the channel with a like, comment, and subscribe if you haven't already.
